hints: Think what happens to the C=C double bond when an alkene polymerises, the pi bond opens to form two new single bonds to neighbours.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond in your mind**
Picture $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCN}$. In addition polymerisation the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ pi bond breaks and each carbon gains one new single bond to the next monomer. So the two carbons become $-\text{CH}_2-$ and $-\text{CH}(\text{CN})-$.

Draw the repeat unit correctly**
Draw $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CN})-$ with square brackets around it and short continuation bonds going through the brackets at each side. That shows this unit repeats many times to give poly(acrylonitrile).
Final answer: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CN})-$ shown inside brackets with continuation bonds through the brackets.

hints: Focus on what attacks the carbonyl carbon in step 1 and what happens to the C=O pi bond, addition across the double bond by a nucleophile.
walkthrough:
Spot the nucleophile and the polar carbonyl**
In step 1, $\text{CN}^-$ from $\text{HCN}$ / $\text{KCN}$ attacks the slightly positive carbon of the polar $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$. The $\text{C}=\text{O}$ pi bond breaks and a new $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond forms, with $\text{H}^+$ added later. Addition of a nucleophile across $\text{C}=\text{O}$ is nucleophilic addition.

hints: Start by marking the polarity of the carbonyl group, which end is delta positive and where the pi electrons will move when attacked.
Remember the cyanide ion uses its lone pair on carbon to form the new C-C bond, leaving a negative charge on oxygen in the intermediate.
Think how that negatively charged oxygen is neutralised in the second stage to give the hydroxynitrile product.
walkthrough:
Set up the polar carbonyl**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ double bond up onto O. This shows the pi electrons moving onto oxygen when the carbon is attacked.

Attack by cyanide to make the alkoxide**
$\text{N}\equiv\text{C}:^-$ has a lone pair on carbon. Draw a curly arrow from that lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of the carbonyl. A new $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond forms and you get the intermediate $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{O}^-)\text{CN}$, with the negative charge on oxygen.

Protonate to finish the hydroxynitrile**
Now the $\text{O}^-$ is strongly basic. Draw a curly arrow from its lone pair to $\text{H}^+$ (from $\text{HCN}$). This forms the $\text{O}-\text{H}$ bond and gives the final product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\delta+$ on C and $\delta-$ on O of C=O, curly arrow from C=O to O, curly arrow from lone pair on C of $:\text{CN}^{-}$ to carbonyl C to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{O}^{-})\text{CN}$ intermediate.
Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ (+ $\text{CN}^{-}$ regenerated if $\text{HCN}$ used as proton source).

hints: Compare step 2 starting material $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ with product $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCN}$, what small molecule has been lost from adjacent carbons.
walkthrough:
Recognise loss of water**
Look closely: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ loses $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ from adjacent carbons to form $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCN}$. That is dehydration, an elimination of water to form an alkene. The classic dehydrating conditions are heating with concentrated sulfuric or phosphoric acid, or passing vapour over hot aluminium oxide.
Final answer: heat with conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ or conc. $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ OR heat with $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$

hints: Read the wavenumber under peaks S and T from Fig. 6.3 and match each value to the closest range in Table 6.1.
walkthrough:
Match wavenumbers to bonds**
Peak S is at about $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Table 6.1 shows only nitrile $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ at $2200-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, a perfect match for $\text{W}$ which contains $\text{CN}$. Peak T is at about $1600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Table 6.1 shows alkene $\text{C}=\text{C}$ at $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, matching the $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-$ part of $\text{W}$.
Final answer: S is $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ and T is $\text{C}=\text{C}$

hints: Think what stays the same and what is different when two molecules are stereoisomers, connectivity versus spatial arrangement.
walkthrough:
Separate connectivity from geometry**
Imagine two molecules with exactly the same atoms joined in exactly the same order, so they have the same structural formula. If the atoms are arranged differently in 3D space, so they are not superimposable in the same way, that is stereoisomerism.
Final answer: compounds with same structural formula but different arrangement of atoms / groups in space

hints: Consider why groups cannot swap sides around a double bond compared with free rotation around a single bond.
Test $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCN}$ by listing the two groups on each double bond carbon to see why it fails one requirement.
walkthrough:
Lock the double bond**
A $\text{C}=\text{C}$ has a pi bond that prevents rotation. The groups are locked in fixed positions above and below the bond axis. Without this restricted rotation, any different arrangements would quickly interconvert and no stable isomers would exist.

Need two different groups on each carbon**
Even with locked rotation, you only get distinct cis-trans forms if each double bond carbon carries two different groups. In $\text{W}$, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCN}$, the left carbon has two $\text{H}$ atoms, so swapping them gives the same arrangement. That is why $\text{W}$ does not show geometrical isomerism.
Final answer: restricted rotation about the C=C bond AND each C of the C=C has two different atoms / groups attached

hints: Identify the chiral carbon in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ and list its four different groups, then think how to show two mirror images in 3D.
walkthrough:
Find the chiral centre**
The middle carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ is bonded to four different groups: $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CN}$. That makes it a chiral centre, so two optical isomers exist.

Draw mirror images in 3D**
Draw the central C with solid wedge for one bond coming out, hashed wedge for one bond going back, and two normal lines in the plane. Keep the same four groups but swap two positions to create the mirror image. The two structures must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: pair of 3D wedge-dash structures of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ with central C bonded to $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CN}$, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images

hints: Count how many $\text{H}_{2}$ molecules are needed to convert $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ fully to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Add hydrogen across the triple bond**
Reducing a nitrile to a primary amine adds four hydrogen atoms in total: $\text{R}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ becomes $\text{R}-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. That needs $2\text{H}_2$. So write $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, which gives propylamine.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_{2} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$

hints: Look at what happens to the OH group in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ when $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ converts it to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$.
walkthrough:
See the swap of OH for Cl**
The $\text{-OH}$ group is directly replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ with no change to the carbon skeleton. Replacing one atom or group by another is substitution.

hints: Recall which nitrogen nucleophile converts a halogenoalkane into a primary amine.
Remember the special solvent and pressure conditions that favour amine formation and minimise further substitution.
walkthrough:
Choose ammonia as nucleophile**
To change $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ into $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, use excess ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$. The lone pair on nitrogen attacks the $\delta+$ carbon and displaces $\text{Cl}^-$ by nucleophilic substitution.

Use the correct conditions**
Heat the halogenoalkane with ammonia dissolved in ethanol in a sealed tube under pressure. Ethanolic conditions and excess ammonia favour formation of the primary amine and reduce further reaction to secondary amines.

Final answer: reagent: ammonia / $\text{NH}_{3}$
conditions: heat in ethanol under pressure / heat in sealed tube
